title: Quantum vs Classical Erasure: Equal Bounds but Unequal Costs
authors: Jan Neuser, Jake Xuereb, Pharnam Bakhshinezhad, Marcus Huber
abstract: Irreversibility has a fundamental thermodynamic cost, erasing information inevitably generates heat. This connection is quantified by the Landauer bound, which gives the minimum dissipation needed to erase a single bit of information. While this bound applies in both classical and quantum settings, it is saturated only in idealised limits of infinite resources. Here, we provide a unified first principles description of finite-resource erasure in both classical and quantum systems. We begin by proving the communal folklore that in the idealised regime the erasure cost of a bit encoded in a quantum or classical system is the same. Despite this, we show that their practical implementation differs substantially: achieving comparable erasure quality in quantum systems requires more control, larger accessible energy gaps and longer operation times. Classical protocols can achieve the erasure of a comparable quantum protocol under far weaker constraints which we expose in trade-off relations. Our results explain why practical erasure schemes fall short of Landauer's bound and show that classical systems enjoy several fundamental thermodynamic advantages.
summary: This work rigorously compares the minimum energy dissipation required to erase bits of information from quantum versus classical physical systems. It proves that while the ultimate theoretical bound is the same, practical constraints reveal significant thermodynamic advantages for classical encoding schemes. The findings help explain why real-world erasure protocols fall short of ideal bounds.
main_problem: The paper compares the thermodynamic cost (dissipation) required for erasing information encoded in quantum versus classical systems when operating with finite resources.
main_result: While ideal erasure costs are equal, practical implementation shows that classical protocols can achieve comparable erasure quality under significantly weaker operational constraints than quantum ones.
method: The analysis uses first principles thermodynamics, comparing dissipation ($\Delta Q$) derived from the Clausius inequality across various idealized and finite-resource limits for both system types.
model_or_system: Quantum bits are modeled as two-level systems coupled to a thermal bath and work source. Classical bits are encoded in many-body systems or ladder structures, allowing for comparison of their respective erasure protocols.
key_observables: Dissipated heat ($\Delta Q$), Fidelity ($F$), Entropy changes ($\Delta S$), and the Landauer bound.
important_parameters: Finite resources, energy gaps, operation times, and the degree of information erasure ($\epsilon$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on idealized asymptotic limits (infinite steps) and specific Hamiltonian interaction forms for both quantum and classical couplings.
figures_summary: Figures compare dissipation vs. fidelity/error probability curves for quantum and classical protocols, illustrating the trade-offs in resource requirements.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the Landauer bound, develops a unified framework for finite-resource erasure cost comparison using energy conservation constraints, derives specific bounds for both systems, and analyzes performance under realistic limitations like imperfect timing.
why_interesting: It provides quantitative thermodynamic comparisons between quantum and classical information processing limits, which is highly relevant to understanding the fundamental resource costs in open quantum systems.
